title.en: Demeter and Persephone: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter and the Eleusinian Mysteries
title.zh: 得墨忒耳與珀耳塞福涅：德墨忒耳頌歌與厄琉息斯秘儀

texts.period: Homeric Hymn 2 composed 7th-6th c. BCE; principal MS: Leiden, University Library 33 H (15th c.); Eleusinian cult attested c. 750-550 BCE onward

source.archive: Center for Hellenic Studies / Perseus Digital Library
source.work: Homeric Hymns 2 (To Demeter), trans. H. G. Evelyn-White, Loeb, 1914; ed. N. J. Richardson, Oxford 1974

summary.en: Persephone is seized by Hades with Zeus's consent; her mother Demeter halts all growth until Zeus negotiates a two-thirds/one-third division of the year; the goddess founds the Eleusinian Mysteries, whose initiates were promised a better lot after death.
summary.zh: 哈得斯得宙斯默許擄走珀耳塞福涅；得墨忒耳憤而令五穀不生，宙斯遂斡旋，女兒一年三分之二在世、三分之一居冥府；女神創立厄琉息斯秘儀，許入儀者身後得福。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult text; the Eleusinian Mysteries' secret rituale is lost — only public literary versions survive. Nothing restricted is reproduced. [Merged 2026-11-11: the entry 'hymn-demeter' (Homeric Hymn 2, trans. Evelyn-White 1914, Theoi Classical Texts Library, https://www.theoi.com/Text/HomericHymns1.html — verbatim passages on the rape of Persephone and the reunion with Demeter) was folded in as passages 3-4 and the duplicate entry removed; motif world-renewal comes from the folded material.]

passages.text: I begin to sing of rich-haired Demeter, awful goddess — of her and her slim-ankled daughter, whom Aidoneus rapt away, given to him by all-seeing Zeus the loud-thunderer.

Condensed paraphrase of Hymn 371-394: Hades secretly gives Persephone a pomegranate seed to eat, binding her to return; Zeus dispatches Rhea, and mother and daughter are reconciled — one third of the year below with her dark lord, two thirds above with her mother and the other immortals. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hymn 371-394; not verbatim.

passages.text: He caught her up reluctant on his golden car and bare her away lamenting. Then she cried out shrilly with her voice, calling upon her father, the Son of Cronos, who is most high and excellent. But no one, either of the deathless gods or of mortal men, heard her voice, nor yet the olive-trees bearing rich fruit: only tender-hearted Hecate, bright-coiffed, the daughter of Persaeus, heard the girl from her cave, and the lord Helios, Hyperion's bright son, as she cried to her father, the Son of Cronos. But he was sitting aloof, apart from the gods, in his temple where many pray, and receiving sweet offerings from mortal men. So he, that Son of Cronos, of many names, who is Ruler of Many and Host of Many, was bearing her away by leave of Zeus on his immortal chariot — his own brother's child and all unwilling.

But while Demeter was still holding her dear child in her arms, her heart suddenly misgave her for some snare, so that she feared greatly and ceased fondling her daughter and asked of her at once: "My child, tell me, surely you have not tasted any food while you were below? Speak out and hide nothing, but let us both know. For if you have not, you shall come back from loathly Hades and live with me and your father, the dark-clouded Son of Cronos and be honoured by all the deathless gods; but if you have tasted food, you must go back again beneath the secret places of the earth, there to dwell a third part of the seasons every year: yet for the two parts you shall be with me and the other deathless gods.

texts.canonical_translation: H. G. Evelyn-White, Homeric Hymns, Loeb 57 (1914); scholarly translation in Helene P. Foley, The Homeric Hymn to Demeter (Princeton, 1994)

narrative.en:
The Hymn (495 dactylic lines) is the fullest continuous Greek narrative of abduction, grief, and negotiated return.

THE ABDUCTION. Persephone, daughter of Demeter, is playing with the daughters of Okeanos, gathering flowers — roses, crocuses, violets, iris, hyacinth — on the Nysian plain. Earth, at Zeus's secret instruction, produces a marvelous narcissus as a snare. As the girl reaches for it, the earth opens; Hades bursts out on his deathless horses, seizes her, and carries her wailing down through the gates of the west. She cries to her father and to the immortals, but no voice heeds her except Hekate's, who hears from her cave with torches lit, and Helios, who sees all and later tells Demeter the truth: the abduction was not the kidnapper's plan alone but Zeus's gift to his brother.

THE GRIEF. For nine days Demeter wanders with flaming torches, neither eating nor washing. Hekate runs to meet her, but can only tell what she heard. From Helios Demeter learns the full crime; furious at the gods, she withdraws from Olympos and comes to Eleusis in the guise of an old woman, sitting in sorrow by the 'maiden's well' (the Parthenion). The daughters of Keleos, lord of Eleusis, find her and lead her to their mother Metaneira; the disguised goddess nurses the infant Demophoon, secretly anointing him with ambrosia and burning away his mortality in the hearth at night — she would make him ageless, a god. Metaneira, spying at night, screams and breaks the ritual: the child cannot now be immortal. Demeter reveals herself, demands a temple and altar at Eleusis, and withdraws her rites.

THE FAMINE. In wrath against Zeus, Demeter 'who brings the seasons' destroys the year's seed; the oxen drag useless ploughs; the whole race of men would have perished of famine, and the gods would have lost their honours and sacrifices. Zeus sends Iris, then one by one all the gods, bearing gifts; Demeter will not lift the curse until she sees her daughter with her own eyes. Zeus therefore sends Hermes to Hades, who agrees — but smilingly, as Persephone is about to ascend, gives her a pomegranate seed to eat, 'secretly and deliberately', so that she must return to him for a third of each year.

THE SETTLEMENT AND END. Mother and daughter embrace; Demeter, learning of the seed, accepts the arrangement. Through the stern command of Rhea, sent down from Olympos by Zeus, the goddesses are reconciled: Persephone spends two-thirds of the revolving year with her mother and the immortals, one-third below; the earth's increase returns, and Demeter restores abundance to the ploughlands. She then returns to Olympos, but first she calls the princes of Eleusis — Triptolemos, Diokles, Eumolpos, and Keleos — and shows them her rites, 'awful mysteries which none may transgress, pry into, or utter; for deep awe of the gods checks the voice'. Blessed is the mortal who has seen them, the Hymn ends: the initiate shares a better lot below; the uninitiated, dying, gets the opposite.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative is the charter myth of the Eleusinian Mysteries, the panhellenic cult whose initiates (from across the Greek world, including slaves and women) swore ritual secrecy; it structures the women's Thesmophoria festival at Athens (which re-enacted fasts and used pig-offerings aitiologically); it explains the agricultural year as a mother-daughter rhythm; it gives Greek marriage its anthropological image — a daughter 'abducted' with paternal consent into the husband's house; and, uniquely among public Greek texts, it attaches eschatological reward to initiatory knowledge. The secret dramatization at Eleusis (reconstructed from archaeology and later Christian polemic) is lost and must not be confounded with the Hymn.
narrative.zh: 珀耳塞福涅與大洋女兒們在尼薩原野採花，大地按宙斯密令生出奇妙水仙為餌；哈得斯裂地而出，攜女入冥，唯赫卡忒聞聲、赫利俄斯見事。得墨忒耳執火炬遍尋九日，怒離奧林波斯，化身老嫗至厄琉息斯王家，哺乳嬰兒得謨福翁，欲以夜火焚其凡性；母后撞破，女神現真身，命建廟。遂降饑饉，牲祭絕於諸神。宙斯屢遣使不得，乃命赫爾墨斯赴冥府；哈得斯微笑授石榴籽一粒，女遂須每年歸冥三月。瑞亞降旨和解：女居上界三分之二，下界三分之一；五穀復生。女神召厄琉息斯諸王子，授以『不可窺、不可傳』之奧儀；入儀者身後得福，未入者不然。秘儀儀程今已失傳，文獻所存僅此公開敘事。

functions: Charter myth of the Eleusinian Mysteries (initiatory secrecy and afterlife promise)
Aitia for the Thesmophoria and the agricultural cycle
Cultural model of marriage-as-abduction under paternal consent
Rare public Greek eschatology: differential fate of initiates and non-initiates

variants.name: Orphic version (Zagreus-Dionysos and Persephone's line)
variants.text_tradition: Orphic fragments (e.g. OF 58, 299 Bernabe); Derveni Papyrus; late antique Neoplatonist citations
variants.summary: In Orphic theology Persephone mates with Zeus and bears Dionysos Zagreus, who is dismembered by Titans; humankind, born from the Titans' ashes, carries both Titanic guilt and Dionysian essence — a descent-and-restoration soteriology rather than a seasonal myth.

variants.name: Arcadian 'Despoina' cult (Lykosoura)
variants.text_tradition: Pausanias, Description of Greece 8.37-38 (2nd c. CE)
variants.summary: A closely parallel mystery cult of Demeter and an unnamed daughter ('Despoina', 'the Mistress') with Artemis and Anytos; the child of Demeter and Poseidon in horse-form. Shows the Eleusinian story is one local, panhellenized form of a wider family of mother-daughter mysteries.

variants.name: Sicilian and South Italian versions
variants.text_tradition: Pindar, fragments; Diodorus Siculus 5.2-5; coin iconography of Enna
variants.summary: Persephone is carried off near Enna/Henna in Sicily's lake meadow, and the island claims the rape and the foundation of cult; Diodorus (himself Sicilian) renders the myth as an allegory of the grain cycle. Underwrites strong Sicilian/Italian mystery cults of Persephone and Dionysos.

variants.name: Thesmophoria liturgical narrative
variants.text_tradition: Athenian women's festival (attested by scholia to Lucian, Dialogue of the Courtesans 2.1; Aristophanes, Thesmophoriazusae)
variants.summary: The women's festival preserves the ritual sequence the Hymn reflects — fasting, obscenity (iambe's jokes), piglets thrown into pits whose rot is mixed with seed-corn — narratively reorganized as Demeter's search, grief, and restoration.

Principal MS: Leiden, Universiteitsbibliotheek 33 H, 15th c. Standard edition: N. J. Richardson, The Homeric Hymn to Demeter, Oxford 1974.

title.en: Heracles: Madness, the Twelve Labors, and Apotheosis
title.zh: 赫拉克勒斯：瘋癲、十二勞役與成神

region.en: Tiryns / Mycenae, Argolid, Greece (symbolic pin for the pan-Hellenic cycle)
region.zh: 希臘阿爾戈利斯提任斯／邁錫尼（泛希臘神話圈象徵性定位）

texts.period: Cycle attested from 8th-7th c. BCE epics; coherent prose retelling in Apollodorus' Bibliotheca 2.4.12-2.7.7 (1st-2nd c. CE; principal MS: Laurentianus 66, 4, 14th c.)

source.work: Apollodorus, The Library 2.4-2.7 (trans. J. G. Frazer, Loeb 121, 1921)

summary.en: Driven mad by Hera, Heracles kills his own family; to expiate, he serves Eurystheus and performs twelve labors — lion, hydra, hind, boar, stables, birds, bull, mares, belt, cattle, apples, Cerberus — then dies on Oeta's pyre and is taken up to Olympos.
summary.zh: 赫拉所遣瘋癲之下，赫拉克勒斯手刃親族；為贖罪服侍歐律斯透斯，歷十二勞役——獅、蛇、鹿、豬、牛廄、鳥、牛、母馬、腰帶、牛群、金蘋果、三頭犬——終於俄塔山火中成神。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary material; classification 'myth' (not 'religious') because Heracles' cult-cycle narrative circulated as heroic legend; note reasoning per README. [Merged 2026-11-11: the earlier entry 'heracles-labors' (Bulfinch, The Age of Fable, 1855, Project Gutenberg eBook #3327 — condensed paraphrase of the Nemean lion and Lernaean hydra labors) was folded in as passages 3-4 and the duplicate entry removed.]

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Apollodorus 2.4.12-2.5.1: Hera sends a madness in which Heracles hurls his children (and Megara's) into the fire; when the fit passes, he seeks purification from Delphi, where the Pythia renames him 'Glory of Hera' (Herakles) and orders him to serve Eurystheus for twelve years and perform whatever labors he is commanded. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Apollodorus 2.4.12-2.5.1; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Apollodorus 2.6.2-2.7.7: to fetch the golden apples of the Hesperides Heracles holds up the sky for Atlas, who fetches the fruit; to bring the hound Cerberus up from Hades he wrestles the shade of Meleager and frees Theseus, then presents the dog to the terrified Eurystheus, who returns it to the underworld. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Apollodorus 2.6.2-2.7.7; not verbatim.

passages.text: Heracles, born to Zeus and the mortal woman Alcmene, drew the lasting hostility of Zeus's wife, who persecuted him from the cradle onward. Through her contrivance he was placed under the authority of his cousin Eurystheus and made to obey whatever that cousin commanded — a chained series of desperate feats the later ages counted as the twelve labors. The first task was to strip the skin from a monstrous lion that was ravaging the valley of Nemea. When club blows and arrows proved useless against the beast's hide, Heracles closed with it and throttled it with his bare hands. He then brought the whole carcass back on his shoulders; Eurystheus, so shaken by this proof of the hero's strength, ordered that future reports be delivered outside the town walls.

The next commission was to destroy the Hydra, which laid waste the countryside of Argos from its lair in a swamp near the well of Amymone. The creature had nine heads, and the middle one could not be killed; its defense was self-renewal, for with every head Heracles cut away, two sprang up in its place. The task became possible only through teamwork — his faithful servant Iolaus burned away each severed stump so no new heads could rise, and the one immortal head was finally buried beneath a massive rock. Even this victory brought him no lasting peace; harder labors, from the Augean stables to the golden apples of the Hesperides, still lay ahead.

texts.canonical_translation: J. G. Frazer, Apollodorus: The Library, Loeb 121-122 (1921)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING. Zeus fathers Herakles on Alkmene while impersonating her husband Amphitryon; Hera, jealous from birth, sends two serpents to strangle the infant, who strangles them instead. Herakles marries Megara, daughter of King Kreon of Thebes, and has children. Hera now strikes him with madness (as dramatized in Euripides' Herakles): in the fit he kills Megara and his sons, and some accounts add his brother Iphikles' children. When sanity returns, the seer, priestess at Delphi (the Pythia), and oracle together impose expiation: he must go to Tiryns, call himself by the name 'Herakles' ('Glory of Hera' — the etymology records the goddess's paradoxical ownership of the hero), and serve the king Eurystheus for twelve years, performing whatever labors are commanded, after which he will become immortal.

THE TWELVE LABORS. (1) The Nemean lion, invulnerable to iron, he strangles and wears its skin; Eurystheus thereafter hides in a bronze jar. (2) The Lernaean hydra, whose heads regrow when cut — with his nephew Iolaos he burns each neck-stump, buries the immortal head under a rock, and dips his arrows in the gall; Eurystheus disallows the labor because of the helper. (3) The Ceryneian hind with golden horns, sacred to Artemis, chased for a year and taken alive. (4) The Erymanthian boar, driven into deep snow and carried back alive. (5) The stables of Augeias, cleaned in a day by diverting the rivers Alpheios and Peneios — denied payment, he sacked Elis; this labor too was disallowed (he demanded wages). (6) The Stymphalian birds, bronze-feathered, driven from the marsh by Athena's rattle and shot down. (7) The Cretan bull, father (by Pasiphae) of the Minotaur, brought alive to Eurystheus and released to wander Marathon. (8) The man-eating mares of Diomedes of Thrace, fed their master to tame them. (9) The war-belt of the Amazon queen Hippolyte — taken (in most versions) after a treacherous brawl. (10) The cattle of the three-bodied Geryon at the far west, past the Pillars he sets up (Gibraltar/Ceuta), driving the herd home through Italy, where cattle-thieves and giants are killed along the way. (11) The golden apples of the Hesperides in Atlas' garden: he holds the sky while Atlas fetches them, tricks the Titan into taking the burden back, and brings the apples to Eurystheus, who returns them to the Hesperides; on the way he frees the chained Prometheus (whose advice steers the episode). (12) Kerberos: he descends at Taenarum, learns courtesy from the shades (Meleager's story of Atalanta; the freeing of Theseus, who is stuck fast), wrestles the hound with bare hands, and brings it up — Eurystheus leaps into his jar, and the hound goes back below.

AFTERMATH AND END. Freed labors, Herakles continues parerga: rescues Hesione at Troy, sacks Pylos, fights the river-god Acheloos for Deianira, and crosses the world in chains of service to Omphale at Sardis. Deianira, jealous, heedlessly sends him a robe soaked in the centaur Nessos' poisoned blood (as Sophocles' Trachiniae dramatizes); it burns his flesh. He builds his own pyre on Mount Oita, and Philoktetes lights it for the reward of the bow. The mortal part burns away; the divine part ascends: Hera reconciles (in late versions by nursing him), and Herakles marries Hebe on Olympos, while the image of the dead hero is worshipped in temples as Herakles the god (Heraikles). Eurystheus, outlived, is defeated by the Herakleidai, his descendants' return aition for the Dorian settlements.

FUNCTIONS. The cycle makes Herakles the panhellenic culture-hero: monster-slayer who clears land, sea, and the edges of the world for colonization (his routes map Greek trade to Gades, the Pontos, and Africa); founder of the Olympic games and of royal genealogies (the Herakleidai); the paradigmatic human who by toil (ponoi) wins immortality — the ideological bridge between mortal suffering and divine reward, ritually echoed at his shrines and in sympotic song.
narrative.zh: 宙斯化形近阿爾克墨涅而生赫拉克勒斯；赫拉自襁褓即遣蛇加害，後遣瘋癲使英雄殺妻兒。得諭示：往提任斯服歐律斯透斯十二年，行其所命之勞役，方可成神。遂歷十二役：一扼涅墨亞獅；二焚九頭蛇許德拉；三獲刻呂涅亞金角鹿；四擒厄律曼托斯野豬；五一日清奧革阿斯牛廄；六驅斯廷法利斯怪鳥；七縛克里特公牛；八馴色雷斯食人馬；九取亞馬孫女王腰帶；十驅革律翁紅牛過西極；十一代阿特拉斯擎天取赫斯珀里得斯金蘋果；十二自塔納隆下冥府擒三頭犬刻耳柏洛斯。後因涅索斯毒血之衣，於俄塔山自焚；凡軀燼滅，神性升天，娶赫柏，受享廟祀。此圈將英雄塑為清辟妖獸、開疆拓土之文化英雄，兼奧林匹亞賽會創立者、多利安諸王族始祖，並示『以勞致不死者』之範型。

functions: Panhellenic culture-hero cycle: clearing the world of monsters and aitiologizing colonization routes
Founding myth for the Olympic games and Dorian royal genealogies (Herakleidai)
Paradigm of mortal toil rewarded with immortality; ideology of expiation after pollution

variants.name: Peisandros of Rhodes, Heracleia (epic, c. 600 BCE)
variants.text_tradition: Fragmentary epic, PEG (Kinkel) frags.; papyrus scraps
variants.summary: The earliest fixed twelve-labor sequence, cited (Pausanias 9.11.2) as the reason the labors are now counted twelve; survives only in fragments, so the sequence is partly reconstructed from citation.

variants.name: Sophocles, Trachiniae
variants.summary: Retells the ending through Deianira's tragedy: the Nessos robe, Heracles' agony on Oita, and the apotheosis left offstage — foregrounding human error rather than divine plan.

variants.name: Euripides, Herakles
variants.summary: Places the madness-murder after the labors (reversing the chronological order of the prose tradition) and emphasizes Theseus' role in restoring the broken hero — an ethics-of-friendship recasting.

variants.name: Scythian version (Herodotus 4.8-10)
variants.summary: In the Scythian aition Herakles herds Geryon's cattle through the northern steppe, fathers Skythes on a half-serpent local goddess, and the triple sons' bow-test founds the Skythian royal line — a colonizing appropriation of the Greek cycle.
